newsitem.title: UK: Convertible bonds to accelerate in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Convertible bonds to accelerate in Latin America.

text.p: Convertible bonds have yet to catch fire in Latin America, but as equity markets in the region continue to rise, bankers say the rate of convertible issues could begin to accelerate by the end of this year.
For the past 18 months, investment banks have urged Latin American corporations to raise funds with convertible bonds, a sector that has flourished in almost every other part of the world.

Latin American convertibles would probably be well received by investors, yet with some stock markets in the region still below levels reached before the Mexican peso crisis in late 1994, many corporations are reluctant to dilute share holdings, bankers said.

"If stock markets move back (up) to pre (Mexican) peso crisis levels and/or if the debt market starts looking less attractive, we'll start to see some deals," said one banker. "Substantial demand is definitely there for Latin American equity-linked paper."

"Convertible issues could come to the market later this year or in 1998, especially if credit spreads remain as tight as they've been. Then companies will have an incentive to issue convertibles," added a convertible analyst with a major U.S. investment bank.
Convertible bonds provide a low-risk alternative to gain exposure in equity markets. They pay a relatively low coupon, but give investors the option to swap the bonds for shares.
To date, there have been only a handful of such deals in Latin America, mostly from Argentina and Mexico. Peru and Chile have also tested the waters.
Issuance of mandatory convertible bonds, like the $356.6 million deal recently issued by SBC Communications Inc of Telfonos de Mxico SA ADRs recently, are also likely to gather pace, bankers said.
But because mandatory bonds automatically convert into shares, there is more downside risk so they are typically less attractive to investors, they said.
The total convertible market in Latin America is only about $4 billion, Katalin Tischhauser, head of convertible research at SBC Warburg, noted.
"That's tiny," she said. "The products are not well known to issuers in the region and there's some resistance on the part of Latin American corporates to dilute their equity.

"There are a lot of corporates there that can and will issue convertibles, but it will take a lot of marketing and explaining on the part of the investment banks. The demand for equity-linked products has been there for the past year or so," she added.
Barring another currency crisis or other financial disaster in the region, Tischhauser said she expects 1997 and 1998 to be a strong growth period for the sector.

Borrowing constraints and the existence of pre-emptive rights in some countries have hampered growth, but the biggest hurdle has been the tight credit spreads that have provided a disincentive for Latin American issuers to tap into convertibles, bankers said.
They reckon that the first straight convertible bond deals probably will come from the regions' biggest stock markets, Mexico, Argentina, Brazil and Chile.

"I would think (Latin American convertible bonds) from those countries would be well received by investors. It's a chicken's way to play the market," said Joe MacHatton, Latin America equity strategist with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"We believe the stock markets in Latin America, in general, are fairly priced. We might see gains of about 10 to 15 percent in the next 12 months," he said. --London newsroom +44 171 542-8863
